concept.name: American-style option
concept.definition: An option that the holder may exercise at any time on or before the expiration date; all standardized U.S. exchange-traded equity options use American-style exercise.
concept.intuition: An American option is a standing offer: any day before expiry, the holder can invoke the strike and take or deliver the underlying.
concept.mechanics: Early exercise is a right, not an obligation, and exercising early forfeits any remaining time value, so holders usually sell rather than exercise; early exercise of a call becomes rational mainly to capture an impending dividend, and of a deep in-the-money put to receive strike proceeds sooner. Because the writer can be assigned at any time, short American options carry early-assignment risk.
concept.failure_modes: Writers who ignore dividend dates or deep-in-the-money scenarios can be assigned early at inopportune times, e.g., losing stock plus dividend entitlements or facing unexpected margin and stock-delivery obligations.
concept.misconceptions: The label has nothing to do with geography or where the option trades — it names the exercise style; and early exercise is rarely optimal for the holder despite being always available, because it discards time value.
concept.example: A holder of an American-style OICX July 60 call can instruct their broker to buy 100 shares at $60 on any trading day up to the July expiration, whereas a writer of that call can be assigned on any such day.
